hops.title: Ask it: which animal feels its way in the dark?
hops.text: Ask your child, "Which animal uses its nose like a feely bag?" Cheer every guess, then share the star-nosed mole. It lives in dark tunnels, and twenty-two wiggly pink rays ring its nose. About 25,000 tiny touch domes cover the rays and help the mole find food by touch where eyes are no help.

sources.citation: Catania, K. C. (1995). Structure and innervation of the sensory organs on the snout of the star-nosed mole. Journal of Comparative Neurology, 351(4), 536-548. PMID: 7721982.
Catania, K. C. (2011). The sense of touch in the star-nosed mole: from mechanoreceptors to the brain. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 366(1581), 3016-3025. PMID: 21969683.

Catania, K. C., & Kaas, J. H. (1997). Somatosensory fovea in the star-nosed mole: behavioral use of the star in relation to innervation patterns and cortical representation. Journal of Comparative Neurology, 387(2), 215-233. PMID: 9336224.

image.caption: A star-nosed mole finds food in dark tunnels by touch, using 22 fleshy nose rays covered in tiny touch domes.

hops.title: Point at it: a rug foot and a tile foot
hops.text: Tomorrow morning, stand together with one bare foot on a rug and the other on a tile floor. Which foot feels cooler? Tile can feel cooler even when it is the same temperature as the rug, because it draws warmth from your foot faster. It is the spoon trick again, underfoot.

sources.citation: Urone, P. P., & Hinrichs, R. (2022). College Physics 2e, Section 14.5: Conduction. OpenStax, Rice University.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Parent and child seen from behind standing barefoot where a woven rug meets a tile floor, the parent on the rug and the child on the tile.
image.caption: Tile can feel cooler than a rug at the same temperature because it draws warmth from your feet faster.

hops.title: Compare it: a toothbrush and a comb
hops.text: Hold up a toothbrush next to a wide-toothed comb. The bristles crowd shoulder to shoulder; the comb teeth stand far apart. Fingertips are like the toothbrush. Scientists estimated that a small patch of fingertip skin has about four times as many touch-sensing nerve fibers as a same-size patch of palm. That helps fingertips tell tiny bumps apart.

sources.citation: Johansson, R. S., & Vallbo, A. B. (1979). Tactile sensibility in the human hand: relative and absolute densities of four types of mechanoreceptive units in glabrous skin. The Journal of Physiology, 286, 283-300. PMID: 439026.
Clark, M. A., Douglas, M., & Choi, J. (2018). Biology 2e, Section 36.2: Somatosensation. OpenStax, Rice University.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A toothbrush with tightly packed bristles lying beside a wide-toothed comb on a wooden table.
image.caption: Closely packed touch sensors help fingertips tell tiny bumps apart, much as crowded bristles outnumber comb teeth.
